Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: 'Explosion or bang sounds' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional history not represented elsewhere. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal/home-based threat, emotional closeness, family comments, shame, weakness, and hypervigilance for someone entering the home. An explosion-specific trigger pulls toward a very different trauma context and is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a distraction strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the selected items. The maladaptive strategy set otherwise reflects avoidance and conflict-generation, while the connected nodes emphasize home intrusion vigilance, bodily reenactment, shame, weakness, and loss of trust. Because Maladaptive Strategies is strongly linked to Triggers and somewhat to Threat/Negative Appraisals here, a severe self-injurious coping item stands out as insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and item pattern.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking Conflict' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The patient's trauma is intimate partner physical abuse, and the other nodes describe hypervigilance, shame, weakness, loss of trust, and avoidance. Deliberately creating interpersonal conflict is a marked shift in style that is not supported by the accompanying threat, memory, appraisal, or trigger items, making this maladaptive strategy clinically incoherent in this profile.

vignette:
María Elena had been a pharmacist for forty-three years, the kind who remembered every regular customer's blood pressure medication and asked after their grandchildren. That was before the night her husband, Roberto, came home from his brother's funeral and turned on her with a fury she had never seen in thirty-eight years of marriage. He shoved her against the kitchen counter, then pinned her to the floor with his knee on her chest, his hand clamped over her mouth as she struggled to breathe. She remembered it not as a story but as a series of frozen images: the crack of her head against the cabinet, the pattern of the linoleum tiles pressed against her cheek, the way his wedding ring dug into her lips. Whenever the memory surfaced, her body would lock into that same position-shoulders hunched, jaw clenched, arms pinned at her sides-as though she were still there on the cold floor. The shame that followed was immediate and crushing: she was a pharmacist, a woman who had raised three children and managed a household, and yet she had not fought back, had not screamed, had not even called the police afterward.

Now, at seventy-four, María Elena still worked three days a week at the same pharmacy, but she had come to believe she was no longer capable of the things that had once defined her. When a customer made an offhand comment about family-a joke about a difficult mother-in-law, a complaint about a sibling-she felt a surge of heat in her chest and a ringing in her ears, her body tensing as though Roberto might appear from behind the vitamin aisle. She had lost her faith in people entirely; it seemed to her that anyone could turn violent without warning, that kindness was merely a mask. The weakness she felt was so complete that she could not stand to look at her own body in the mirror, because when she did, she saw only the woman who had lain helpless on the kitchen floor.

The door at the pharmacy was heavy and pneumatic, but whenever it slammed shut-a delivery driver, a teenager in a hurry-María Elena's heart would race and her gaze would dart to the entrance, scanning for threat. She found herself listening constantly for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home, even during the day when Roberto was at work. Her body felt perpetually tense, as though bracing for a blow that had not yet landed. This hypervigilance made her avoid other people altogether outside of work; she stopped attending church, declined invitations from her daughters, and told herself she was simply tired. When she did feel a strong emotion-anger at a rude customer, sadness during a commercial about an anniversary-she immediately pushed it away, because she had come to believe that feeling anything deeply was dangerous, that it would crack her open and reveal the pathetic person she had become.

The shame and the belief in her own weakness made the memories more vivid and more frequent. A door slamming at the pharmacy would trigger not just a racing heart but a full sensory flashback: the smell of floor cleaner, the pressure of Roberto's knee, the shame of her own stillness. And each time she relived it, she felt more convinced that she was no longer capable, that she had lost herself completely. This cycle tightened over the months. The more she avoided her feelings and her own body, the more she confirmed to herself that she was weak, and the more she scanned for danger. She watched for signs in Roberto's voice, in the way he walked through the door, in the silence of the house. She caught herself listening for footsteps in the hallway at night, even though he had never hurt her again after that single night.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning at the pharmacy when a young woman came to the counter, crying, and asked for a referral to a counselor. María Elena had filled the prescription without a word, her hands shaking, and had spent the rest of the day avoiding the memory of her own helplessness. That evening, alone in the bathroom, she caught a glimpse of her face in the mirror and did not recognize the woman staring back. She was terrified that she would never feel safe again, and she was desperate to believe she could.
